desc:
The range of a subarray is its largest value minus its smallest value (a single element has range 0). Return the sum of the ranges of all non-empty contiguous subarrays of nums, taken modulo 1,000,000,007.

Example: for [1, 3, 3] the subarrays [1,3] and [1,3,3] have range 2 and all others have range 0, so the answer is 4.
constraints: Return the sum modulo 1,000,000,007 (the true sum is never negative)
hints: Looking at all O(n<sup>2</sup>) subarrays and tracking a running max and min works for small inputs. Try to split the answer into (sum of maxima) minus (sum of minima).

For the sum of maxima, ask for each element how many subarrays it is the maximum of. If nums[i] can extend a steps to the left and b steps to the right before meeting a bigger element, it is the maximum of a * b subarrays.

Break ties so each subarray has one owner (strictly greater on one side, greater-or-equal on the other). Compute both distances with monotonic stacks. The minima work the same way, or negate the array and reuse the code.
editorial: The range sum equals (sum over all subarrays of the maximum) minus (sum over all subarrays of the minimum). For the maximum, count how many subarrays each element decides. Index i is the owner of exactly (i - left) * (right - i) subarrays, where left is the nearest index on the left with a value ≥ nums[i] and right the nearest index on the right with a value > nums[i]; the unequal comparisons make every subarray counted once even with duplicates.

A monotonic stack finds all left values in one left-to-right pass and all right values in one right-to-left pass. The contribution of i is nums[i] times its count. For the minima, apply the same function to the negated array: the sum of minima is minus the sum of maxima of the negated values, so range sum = f(nums) + f(-nums). Total time O(n), space O(n). The exact sum can be huge, so reduce modulo 109+7 at the end (Python integers do not overflow; in other languages reduce per term).
